passages.text: PLAGUE, or PESTILENCE, a very acute and contagious disease, attended with a fever, buboes or swellings in the groin and armpits, carbuncles, and livid spots upon the skin.
It is the most fatal of all diseases; in the great plague of London in 1665 there died, according to the bills of mortality, near 70,000 persons.
The disease is supposed to arise from a peculiar corruption of the air, which first breaks out in Egypt and the Levant, and is thence carried by ships to other countries.
It is communicated chiefly by contact with infected persons, and by goods, as cotton, wool, and clothes, which retain the infection for a long time.

For this reason ships and goods from infected places are kept in quarantine, that is, separated for forty days before they may land, by which means the plague has been kept out of Britain for more than a century.
The cure is attempted by sweating medicines, cordials, and by bringing the buboes to suppuration with poultices; but the greater part of those seized perish, whatever be done.
Plague is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Symptoms include fever, weakness and headache.

There are three forms of plague. In bubonic plague, the lymph nodes swell into painful buboes, most often in the groin or armpit. Septicemic plague infects the blood, and pneumonic plague infects the lungs.
Bubonic plague is mainly spread by the bites of infected fleas from small animals such as rats. Pneumonic plague can spread between people through infected droplets in the air.
The bacterium was identified in 1894 by Alexandre Yersin during an epidemic in Hong Kong.
Plague is treated with antibiotics such as gentamicin and doxycycline. Without treatment, plague kills 30 to 90% of those infected.
The Black Death of the 14th century caused more than 50 million deaths. Later outbreaks included the Great Plague of London of 1665 to 1666.
Quarantine, from the Italian for forty days, began as a measure against plague in the late Middle Ages.

reasons: Rare terms appear in both: buboes, groin, armpit, quarantine, 1665.
Great Plague of London scores well but covers only one outbreak, so it is a second candidate.

britannica.quote: buboes or swellings in the groin and armpits

wikipedia.quote: the lymph nodes swell into painful buboes, most often in the groin or armpit

alignments.note: Same sign, same word, same places on the body.

alignments.label: The cause

britannica.quote: a peculiar corruption of the air

wikipedia.quote: caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis

alignments.note: Corrupted air is replaced by a bacterium, identified in 1894.

alignments.label: Infected goods

britannica.quote: by goods, as cotton, wool, and clothes, which retain the infection for a long time

wikipedia.quote: spread by the bites of infected fleas from small animals such as rats

alignments.note: Inference: goods and clothes could carry infected fleas, so the observation had a basis. The carrier was the flea, not the cloth.

alignments.label: Contact with the sick

britannica.quote: communicated chiefly by contact with infected persons

wikipedia.quote: Pneumonic plague can spread between people through infected droplets in the air

alignments.note: Only the lung form passes directly between people. The common bubonic form comes from flea bites.

britannica.quote: kept in quarantine, that is, separated for forty days

wikipedia.quote: Quarantine, from the Italian for forty days

alignments.label: London, 1665

britannica.quote: in the great plague of London in 1665

wikipedia.quote: the Great Plague of London of 1665 to 1666

alignments.note: Same outbreak. Wikipedia gives no death count in this passage.

alignments.label: Most die

britannica.quote: the greater part of those seized perish, whatever be done

alignments.note: True in 1797, no longer: antibiotics now cure most patients. Untreated, 30 to 90% still die.

britannica.quote: first breaks out in Egypt and the Levant

alignments.note: Inference: Britain met plague through Levant trade, but the 1797 claim that it starts there has no support in the Wikipedia text.

suggestedQuestions: How did people in 1797 think plague spread?
Did quarantine in 1797 work the same way it does today?
Is plague still as deadly as the 1797 entry says?

How did people in 1797 think plague spre.answer:
Through a corruption of the air that started in Egypt and the Levant and travelled by ship [B3], and then by contact with the sick and with goods such as cotton, wool and clothes [B4].

Wikipedia says bubonic plague is mainly spread by the bites of infected fleas from rats and other small animals, and only the lung form passes between people [W3]. Goods carrying fleas would explain the old observation, but that is an inference.

Did quarantine in 1797 work the same way.answer: The word and the forty days are the same: in 1797 ships and goods from infected places were kept apart for forty days [B5], and Wikipedia traces the word to the Italian for forty days [W7]. The 1797 entry credits quarantine with keeping plague out of Britain for more than a century [B5]. Wikipedia does not say whether that is true.

Is plague still as deadly as the 1797 en.answer: No. In 1797 the greater part of those seized died whatever was done [B6]. Today antibiotics such as gentamicin and doxycycline treat it; without treatment 30 to 90% of those infected still die [W5].
